lead: An AC voltage controller controls the RMS voltage delivered to an AC load without changing the 50 Hz frequency. It is a thyristor switch in series with the load: two SCRs back to back, or one TRIAC. Phase control delays the firing angle in every half cycle. On-off control passes whole cycles and blocks whole cycles. Lamp dimmers, heater and furnace controls, fan regulators and induction-motor soft starters use this idea. The same circuit is also called an AC voltage regulator in some syllabi.
prereq: You need: the SCR and natural commutation (Unit 1), and the firing angle of a controlled rectifier (Unit 2).

blocks.text: The controller is a switch in series with the load, fed from an AC supply of RMS value Vs. Two SCRs connected back to back conduct in opposite half cycles. One TRIAC does the same job; see 5.2 for its gate behaviour.

In phase control the gate pulse is delayed by the firing angle α after each supply-voltage zero crossing. α is measured in radians in the formulas below. The positive SCR conducts from α to the point where its current falls to zero; the negative SCR does the same in the next half cycle. For a resistive load, current falls to zero at the voltage zero, so each half cycle conducts from α to π.

blocks.where: V<sub>rms</sub> is the load RMS voltage; V<sub>s</sub> is the supply RMS voltage; α is the firing angle in radians, 0 ≤ α ≤ π for a resistive load.

blocks.text: On-off control, also called integral-cycle or burst control, gates the switch for n whole cycles and blocks it for m whole cycles. The duty ratio is D = n/(n+m). Over a burst period the RMS voltage is V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D.

Phase control is smooth and fast. The load voltage is a chopped sine, so the supply current contains low-order harmonics. For a resistive load the input power factor equals V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>. At α = 90° this ratio is 0.707; near α = 180° it is very small, because the supply still applies the full voltage V<sub>s</sub> while the load receives almost none of it, so little useful power flows for the supply rating used.

On-off control keeps the current a full sine during the on cycles. Its unwanted frequencies sit at the burst rate and sidebands, not at the low odd harmonics of phase control. The penalty is flicker: lamps visibly blink and motors feel torque pulses when the burst period is long. Large n and m reduce this, but make the response slow.

Choose phase control for lamp dimming and fan speed, where smooth adjustment matters. Choose on-off control for heaters and furnaces, where thermal inertia hides the burst and high power factor during on cycles is welcome.
With a purely resistive load, the conduction angle in each half cycle is π − α. At α = 0 the load gets the full sine. At α = π it gets zero. The simple RMS formula above covers this case.

With an RL load, current lags voltage and cannot stop at the voltage zero. The SCR stays on until the current reaches zero at the extinction angle β. The conduction angle is γ = β − α. During conduction the current is

blocks.where: V<sub>m</sub> is the peak supply voltage; Z = √(R<sup>2</sup> + (ωL)<sup>2</sup>); φ = tan<sup>−1</sup>(ωL/R); θ is angular time; β is the first θ > α where i(θ) = 0.

blocks.text: The resistive RMS formula is not valid for RL loads; you must integrate the load voltage or current over the actual conduction interval. For α below φ, the current from the previous half cycle has not yet fallen to zero when the next SCR receives its gate pulse. That SCR is therefore not forward biased at that instant, a short pulse is lost, and conduction fails to start. Use a wide (continuous) gate pulse, or keep α ≥ φ; with a wide pulse the current becomes continuous and control is lost. Some syllabi call the whole circuit an AC voltage regulator.

items: Lamp dimming: phase control with a TRIAC gives smooth brightness; the filament hides some harmonic effect.
Heater and furnace: on-off control at zero crossing switches at near-zero current, so stress is low; thermal mass smooths the burst.
Fan regulator: a TRIAC phase controller is common; see 5.2.
Induction-motor soft starter: phase control raises RMS voltage gradually, limiting starting current and torque.

figure.caption: RMS output ratio against firing angle for a resistive load. The phase-control curve falls from 1 to 0, and the flat line at 0.707 is on-off control with D = 0.5.

spec.aria: A falling curve shows the RMS output ratio dropping from 1 at zero firing angle to 0 at 180 degrees, with a flat line at 0.707 crossing it exactly at 90 degrees.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 20 Ω resistive load through a single-phase AC voltage controller. Find the RMS output voltage, RMS current and load power for (a) phase control at α = 90°, (b) on-off control with duty cycle D = 0.5.
steps: For a resistive load at α = 90°, α = π/2 rad. The bracket is 1 − (π/2)/π + sin(2×π/2)/(2π) = 1 − 0.5 + sin π/(2π) = 0.5 + 0 = 0.5.
For on-off control, D = 0.5 gives V<sub>rms</sub> = 230 × √0.5 = 162.6 V. The same 20 Ω load takes 8.13 A and 1.32 kW.
examples.answer: Both methods give 162.6 V RMS, 8.13 A and 1.32 kW; phase control adds low-order harmonics, on-off control adds burst-rate flicker.
examples.check:
import math
Vs = 230.0
R = 20.0
alpha = math.pi/2
bracket = 1 - alpha/math.pi + math.sin(2*alpha)/(2*math.pi)
V_a = Vs*math.sqrt(bracket)
I_a = V_a/R
P_a = V_a*I_a/1000
D = 0.5
V_b = Vs*math.sqrt(D)
I_b = V_b/R
P_b = V_b*I_b/1000
print(round(V_a,1))
print(round(I_a,2))
print(round(P_a,2))
print(round(V_b,1))
print(round(I_b,2))
print(round(P_b,2))

traps: Using degrees in a formula that needs radians. α = 90° must be π/2; the bracket is 0.5, so V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = 0.707, not 0.9.
Using the phase-control RMS formula for an RL load. It holds only for a resistive load; for RL integrate over the actual conduction angle.
Confusing on-off duty ratio D with the phase-control ratio V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>. For on-off, V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = √D, so D = 0.5 gives 0.707, not 0.5.
Forgetting that α has a valid range. For a resistive load 0 ≤ α ≤ 180°; for an RL load, a short gate pulse below the load angle may not start conduction.
Treating the TRIAC as a controlled rectifier. In this circuit it conducts in both half cycles; the two-SCR pair is its equivalent.

quiz.q: What two devices can form the series switch in a single-phase AC voltage controller?
quiz.a: Two SCRs connected back to back, or one TRIAC.

quiz.q: Why does phase control give a poor input power factor at large firing angle for a resistive load?
quiz.a: V<sub>rms</sub> falls while the supply voltage stays fixed. For a resistive load PF = V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> = √(1 − α/π + sin(2α)/(2π)); near α = 180° this ratio is small, so the circuit draws little useful power for its RMS current.

quiz.q: A 240 V RMS supply feeds a resistive load through a phase-controlled AC controller at α = 60°. Find V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub> and V<sub>rms</sub>.
An on-off controller has n = 3 conducting cycles and m = 1 blocked cycle. Find D and V<sub>rms</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>.
Why does on-off control avoid the low-order harmonics of phase control, and what problem replaces them?
quiz.a: During on cycles the load current is an unchopped sine, so there is no low-order harmonic from phase chopping. Switching on and off at the burst rate creates sidebands and subharmonics around 50 Hz; lamps flicker and motors pulse.

quiz.q: An RL load has φ = 45°. The controller is fired at α = 30° with a short gate pulse. What can happen?
quiz.a: α = 30° is below the load angle φ = 45°, so the previous SCR is still carrying current when this gate pulse arrives. The incoming SCR is not forward biased at that instant and a short pulse is lost, so the SCR may fail to latch. Use a wider gate pulse or fire at α ≥ φ. The simple resistive formula is invalid here.

quiz.q: State the conduction angle for a resistive load at firing angle α.
quiz.a: π − α radians, or 180° − α, in each half cycle.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, phase-controlled AC controllers appear in soft starters and static VAR systems, while integral-cycle switching is used for high-power heaters. Newer work replaces phase control with PWM AC choppers (see 5.4) when waveform quality matters. Researchers study hybrid on-off and phase schemes to reduce flicker and harmonic current. Search for "AC voltage controller power factor", "integral cycle control", and "TRIAC dimmer harmonics" to go further.
